claims.text: The FeNiCrMn alloy is initially a solid solution without precipitates or second phases.
Lower test temperatures increase the alloy's strength relative to the room-temperature, 10^-3 s^-1 baseline.
Higher strain rates increase the alloy's strength relative to the room-temperature, 10^-3 s^-1 baseline.
Lower test temperatures decrease the alloy's ductility relative to the room-temperature, 10^-3 s^-1 baseline.
Higher strain rates decrease the alloy's ductility relative to the room-temperature, 10^-3 s^-1 baseline.
The temperature- and strain-rate-dependent strength and ductility arise from thermally activated dislocation glide.
The temperature- and strain-rate-dependent strength and ductility arise from thermally activated dislocation cross-slip.
Chemical short-range order influences dislocation glide and cross-slip in this alloy.
Lattice distortion influences dislocation glide and cross-slip in this alloy.
Dislocation density and mobility mediate the effects of test temperature and strain rate on mechanical behavior.
The predicted strength and ductility effect becomes more pronounced at higher temperatures because thermal activation of dislocation mechanisms is enhanced.
Above 400°C, grain-boundary sliding may contribute to the alloy's behavior.
Above 400°C, diffusion-controlled processes may contribute to the alloy's behavior.
Below a strain rate of 10^-3 s^-1, grain-boundary sliding or diffusion-controlled processes may contribute to the alloy's behavior.
Room temperature and a strain rate of 10^-3 s^-1 define the comparison baseline.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis attributes strengthening and ductility loss to lower temperatures, but the predicted outcome also says the effect is more pronounced at higher temperatures. The direction of the temperature dependence is therefore internally inconsistent.

The lowest specified test temperature is 20°C, which is also the room-temperature baseline, so the proposed matrix contains no condition below the baseline with which to directly test the prediction about behavior at lower temperatures.
